summary: This standards-track document defines the Network Control Protocol that sets up and configures NetBIOS Frames (NBF) over PPP links. It applies when an end system connects to a peer system or to the LAN behind that peer.

eli5.summary: Before two computers on a phone line can share files the old Windows way, they agree on the rules using this protocol.

questions: how to run netbios over ppp
what is the ppp netbios frames control protocol
what is name projection in nbfcp
subtitle: How a PPP link agrees to carry NetBIOS Frames (NBF) traffic, including which NetBIOS names the dial-in side claims.

tldr.problem: PPP needs a Network Control Protocol for each network-layer protocol it carries, and NBF (originally called NetBEUI) had none.
tldr.mechanism: NBFCP reuses the LCP packet exchange and defines four configuration options: Name-Projection, Peer-Information, Multicast-Filtering and IEEE-MAC-Address-Required.
tldr.outcome: Once NBFCP reaches the Opened state, NBF datagrams can flow over the link. It suits an end system connecting to a peer or its LAN, not joining two LANs.

today: RFC 2097 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata for this RFC lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 1661, the PPP specification.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
PPP has three parts: a way to wrap datagrams, a Link Control Protocol (LCP) that sets up and tests the link, and a family of Network Control Protocols that set up each network-layer protocol. RFC 2097 defines the control protocol for NBF, the protocol originally called NetBEUI. It is called the NBF Control Protocol, or NBFCP.

The order is fixed. Each end sends LCP packets first. After the link is established, PPP sends NBFCP packets to choose and configure NBF. Once NBFCP reaches the Opened state, NBF datagrams can be sent over the link. The link stays configured until LCP or NBFCP packets close it, or until an external event such as an inactivity timer or an administrator closes it.

The abstract says NBFCP is only applicable for an end system connecting to a peer system or the LAN that peer is on. It is not applicable for connecting two LANs together, because of NetBIOS name limitations and NetBIOS name defense mechanisms.
sections.eli5: Before two computers can talk the old Windows way over a phone line, they use a short getting-ready chat. This RFC is the rulebook for that chat.

sections.title: NBFCP as a Variant of LCP
sections.content:
NBFCP uses the same packet exchange mechanism as LCP and is described as exactly the same as LCP with a few exceptions. NBFCP packets MUST NOT be exchanged until PPP has reached the Network-Layer Protocol phase. Packets that arrive earlier should be silently discarded.

  • One NBFCP packet goes in the Information field of a PPP frame whose Protocol field is hex 803f (NBF Control Protocol).
  • Only Codes 1 through 7 are used: Configure-Request, Configure-Ack, Configure-Nak, Configure-Reject, Terminate-Request, Terminate-Ack and Code-Reject. Other Codes are treated as unrecognized and answered with a Code-Reject.
  • NBFCP has its own set of Configuration Options.

On timeouts, an implementation should be ready to wait for authentication and link quality determination to finish before giving up on a Configure-Ack. Because NetBIOS name defense takes time (typically a minimum of 3 seconds if names are added in parallel), the RFC suggests raising timeouts to 10 seconds when Name-Projection is negotiated.
sections.eli5: The getting-ready chat for this protocol follows the same pattern as the one for the phone line itself. Only the list of things you can agree on is different.

sections.title: Sending NBF Datagrams
sections.content:
No NBF packets may be sent until PPP is in the Network-Layer Protocol phase and NBFCP is Opened. Unless otherwise negotiated, exactly one NBF packet goes in the Information field of a PPP frame whose Protocol field is hex 003f (NBF datagram).

NBF datagrams on PPP have no length field, so the packet MUST NOT carry extra padding octets unless Self-Defining-Padding is negotiated. There is no standard way to fragment and reassemble NBF datagrams, so PPP links supporting NBF MUST allow at least 576 octets in the Information field. The RFC recommends 1500 octets unless the IEEE-MAC-Address-Required option is negotiated.

The RFC notes at least four MAC header styles for NBF: 802.3 Ethernet, 802.5 Token-Ring, DIX Ethernet and FDDI. Because NBF is not routable, some implementations need the IEEE MAC addresses, or even the whole MAC header, to route or bridge NBF packets. Those that need addresses should negotiate IEEE-MAC-Address-Required. NetBIOS gateways may need no MAC fields at all.
sections.eli5: Each message goes in its own envelope, and the envelope has to be at least a certain size. Some helper machines also want the sender and receiver address labels added, so they can ask for them.

sections.title: Name-Projection and NetBIOS Name Defense
sections.content:
NetBIOS names must be unique on a network. To guarantee that, end-system implementations MUST negotiate the Name-Projection option (type 1). The sender of a Configure-Request lists the NetBIOS names it wants the remote peer to add on the remote network. Each name is 16 octets, followed by an Added octet. The option length is 2 plus 17 per name. The length field is one octet, so one option holds at most 14 names; for more, send several Name-Projection options in the same Configure-Request.

If the receiver cannot add all the names, it MUST Configure-Nak with the complete list. Names that were added have Added set to zero; names that failed get a non-zero return code. The sender SHOULD then resend the request with only the names that were added. In a Configure-Request the Added field holds the name type: 01 for a unique name, 02 for a group name. In a Configure-Reject it carries the NetBIOS return code, such as 00 (added), 0D (duplicate name in local name table), 0E (name table full), 16 (name in use on remote NetBIOS) or 19 (name conflict detected).

An implementation that does not attempt to add any names MUST Configure-Reject this option. Because adding names usually takes 3 seconds and PPP may default its restart timer to 3 seconds, the restart timer SHOULD default to 10 seconds when configuring NetBIOS names.
sections.eli5: Every computer needs a name nobody else is using. Joining the line means saying the names you want and hearing back which ones were already taken.

sections.title: Peer-Information and Multicast-Filtering
sections.content:
Peer-Information (type 2) lets a peer share NetBIOS-related details. Negotiating it is not mandatory but is suggested. It carries a one-octet Peer-class, a four-octet Peer-version (two octets major, two octets minor) and an optional Peer-name of at most 32 octets, with a suggested value of the NetBIOS workstation name. With no name the length is 8; otherwise the name is Length minus 8 octets. The classes are 2 (PPP NetBIOS Gateway Server), 4 (PPP Local Access Only Server), 6 (PPP NBF Bridge) and 8 (PPP End-System); the odd values 1, 3, 5 and 7 are reserved for legacy implementations.

Multicast-Filtering (type 3, length 5) negotiates how multicast packets are handled. Some NetBIOS applications use multicasts to talk and need them forwarded; others need none, so it is best to slow the rate. The option holds a two-octet Multicast-Forward-Period in seconds (maximum 60; zero means no maximum period, so all multicasts SHOULD be forwarded; hex FFFF means unknown) and a one-octet Priority (0 means directed packets have priority, 1 means multicast packets do). Peers that rely on every multicast being forwarded SHOULD ask for a period of zero and a priority of one by sending a Configure-Nak.
sections.eli5: The two sides can also introduce themselves, saying what kind of machine they are. They can agree on how often loud broadcast-style messages get passed along.

sections.title: The IEEE-MAC-Address-Required Option
sections.content:
This boolean option (type 4, length 2) lets a peer require that every NBF datagram carry a 12 octet IEEE MAC address header. By default no MAC header is sent, and the NBF information field is equivalent to the data field of 802.3, 802.5 and FDDI frames.

When negotiated, each datagram has a destination MAC address and a source MAC address prepended, then the 802.3/802.5/FDDI data field. The MAC address is in non-canonical form: the first bit sent in each byte is the most significant bit. Because the option is negotiated after the LCP phase, NBF packets MAY exceed the negotiated PPP MRU. An implementation that negotiates it MUST accept NBF packets 12 octets larger than the negotiated MRU.
sections.eli5: Some machines want a proper address label on every message. If both sides agree, each message gets one, and the envelope is allowed to be a little bigger.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC's security section is a single sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo. Authentication, where used, is handled by PPP before NBFCP begins, since NBFCP packets are only exchanged after the link reaches the Network-Layer Protocol phase.
sections.eli5: This RFC does not say anything about keeping the chat secret or checking who is on the line.

items.label: Name-Projection
items.desc: Asks the peer to add NetBIOS names on its network.

items.label: Peer-Information
items.desc: Shares peer class, version and name.

items.label: Multicast-Filtering
items.desc: Negotiates multicast forward period and priority.

items.label: IEEE-MAC-Address-Required
items.desc: Requires a 12 octet MAC header on each NBF datagram.

fields.name: Multicast-Forward-Period
fields.desc: Maximum period in seconds at which multicasts can be sent; maximum 60.

fields.name: Priority
fields.desc: 0 means directed packets have priority, 1 means multicast packets do.
